analysis.one_liner: Bans the gasoline additive MTBE, which leaks from tanks and fouls drinking water.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 28 bipartisan cosponsors, never got a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: MTBE is a fuel additive refiners blend into gasoline so it burns cleaner, but it dissolves easily in water and spreads quickly when gasoline leaks from storage tanks, making wells and drinking water taste and smell bad. This bill would have told the EPA to write rules banning MTBE in gasoline, with three years to phase it out. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drinks water from public systems or private wells, especially in states where gasoline leaks have contaminated groundwater with MTBE. Water utilities and taxpayers would also save cleanup costs over time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households relying on groundwater and wells

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA to write Clean Air Act rules that prohibit MTBE as a fuel additive, removing the chemical that contaminates groundwater when gasoline leaks from storage tanks [S2][S3].
Gives refiners three years to switch, easing the transition away from MTBE [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Refiners and MTBE manufacturers would bear the cost of reformulating gasoline and losing the MTBE market. Consumers could see small changes in gasoline costs depending on what additive replaces MTBE.

drawbacks.text: The three-year phaseout and a flat ban give limited flexibility; the EPA and refiners argued that oxygenate rules in the Clean Air Act made it hard to drop MTBE without a substitute, so a ban could disrupt gasoline supply and prices [S2][S3].
The bill does not address cleanup of MTBE already in groundwater or fund remediation for contaminated water systems [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and cleanup benefit of removing a chemical that spreads quickly into drinking water outweighed the reformulation costs to refiners, which were manageable over a three-year phaseout. The bill's main weakness was that it did nothing about water already contaminated.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 12, 1999 by Rep. Bob Franks with 28 cosponsors split 17 Republicans and 11 Democrats [S1][S4].
Referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce [S5].
On April 28, 1999 referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: MTBE manufacturers and refiners kept selling and using the additive for years longer. Ethanol producers also lost the near-term chance to capture the oxygenate market MTBE would have vacated.

for.name: Rep. Bob Franks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban MTBE as a fuel additive.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Tom Bliley (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in two Congress sessions.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 17 Republicans and 11 Democrats; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the MTBE market, forcing refiners to reformulate gasoline. MTBE's benefit (cleaner combustion) came at the cost of widespread groundwater contamination from leaking storage tanks.

Ethanol was the main substitute oxygenate refiners could use to meet clean-fuel requirements, so an MTBE ban would have created a large new market for ethanol. The bill did not mandate ethanol, so this gain was indirect.
